title: MSP apologises over controversial rape 'demonisation' comments
description: The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of ra
body: The comments have been widely criticised by survivors groups and political opponents who said they downplayed the seriousness and lasting trauma of rape.The SCRA, which comprises support groups in Glasgow, Lanarkshire, Ayrshire and the Western Isles, said the impacts of rape can last a lifetime, and the crime should never be reduced to a theoretical debate. In an open letter the alliance said: "We are not demonising rape. We are naming it."The authors strongly opposed the idea of rape existing on a "spectrum", insisting "there is no hierarchy of rape" and that no survivor should feel compelled to ask whether their experience was serious enough."The letter urged politicians "not to normalise" rape or sexual violence, and "not create hierarchies of harm". While not naming Manivannan, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Violence against Women and Girls, Reem Alsalem, posted on X that rape should never be spoken about in terms of it being a spectrum.Scotland's Children's Minister Siobhan Brown told the BBC's Sunday Show Manivannan's words were misjudged. Scottish Labour and the Scottish Liberal Democrats have also been critical, while the Scottish Conservatives called on the Scottish Greens to suspend the MSP.Meghan Gallacher, the party's equalities spokeswoman, said: "It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences."In a statement issued on Monday afternoon, Manivannan said they were "horrified" that the comments had been "selectively edited in order to mislead people and misrepresent me". "I also accept that my language was abstract in the first place and for that I take full responsibility and am sorry," they said.The MSP said that during the interview they had categorically stated that every rape in every context is equally serious and harmful but this had been "maliciously" left out of clips. They added: "I recognise that the words in the clip shared, without the full context of the conversation, have caused considerable upset. "For that I apologise. I will always stand with and for victims and survivors."Manivannan said they were themselves a survivor of sexual violence and understood the enduring trauma of such an experience. "I would never seek to diminish or dismiss any survivor's experience, or to make anyone feel that their pain was not heard or understood," they added. "I am genuinely sorry to everyone who has been distressed, hurt or triggered by the clips, and by the discussion and coverage that has followed. "Words matter, particularly when speaking about something as deeply personal and painful as sexual violence, and I regret this hurt caused."Manivannan, who was elected as a list MSP representing Edinburgh and Lothians East under Scotland's proportional representation system, said they would welcome the opportunity to meet survivor and advocacy groups to listen to their perspectives.

schema.headline: MSP apologises over controversial rape 'demonisation' comments

title: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer
description: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summerByRob CorpBarbara Metzler and Thomas SpencerBBC VerifyWith more par
body: From Stonehenge to the Serpentine - satellite images show impact of hot, dry summerByRob CorpBarbara Metzler and Thomas SpencerBBC VerifyWith more parts of England set to join Wales as being officially declared to be in drought, BBC Verify has been gathering satellite imagery showing the impact of this year's extreme summer heat.From historic sites and parks to reservoirs and golf courses, the hot, dry weather has changed how large parts of the UK usually look.This year's consecutive heatwaves and above-average temperatures have had a noticeable effect -  even compared with last summer which was the UK's warmest on record.Drop in Welsh reservoir levelAccording to the UK government, almost all reservoirs in England and Wales are officially classed as having water levels below normal or low.Five are exceptionally low - among them Clywedog reservoir in Powys which provides water supplies for parts of the West Midlands.These satellite images show how more of the banks of the reservoir are visible this August compared with the same month last year.Low reservoir levels have not been the primary cause of recent hosepipe bans and drought declarations - which are ultimately triggered by a lack of rain - across large parts of England and Wales.The Environment Agency has reported that reservoir storage is now at 69% in England, which is below the long-term average of 82% for the time of year but higher than during last year's drought.However, in its latest report the agency says water storage levels are above those recorded during similar periods in 2022 and 2025.While Scotland has not been as badly affected as England and Wales, July's rainfall was below average for the south and east of the country, with many areas seeing less than half the long-term average for the month.This has led the Scottish Environment Protection Agency to warn of "significant" water scarcity in the Borders and "moderate scarcity" in areas on the eastern side of Scotland.Brown fairways at Open golf courseHard and dry fairways were a key talking point at golf's Open Championship which was held at Royal Birkdale on Merseyside last month.A side-by-side comparison shows how much greener the fairways appeared in summer 2025 compared with this year.As the BBC reported earlier this month while domestic users face hosepipe restrictions the rules for commercial users - including golf courses - vary.When hosepipe bans are in force sports grounds can use hoses or sprinklers - but only to water grass areas "actively used for play". For golf courses this means the greens and tees can be irrigated but the fairways cannot.Algal blooms in reservoirs and lakesRight in the heart of the UK capital, Hyde Park's famous Serpentine lake was closed for swimming on Monday because of high levels of blue-green algae.Blue-green algae occur naturally, but warm, sunny and settled conditions can help blooms develop. Some can be harmful to people and animals.A similar issue is affecting Killington Reservoir in south Cumbria. Satellite images show a visible change in the water between 24 May and 8 August, where a blue-green algal bloom has been confirmed.Looking at the rest of Hyde Park and what is one of London's prime green spaces is now mostly brown following consecutive heatwaves since May.It's a similar sight in south Wiltshire where the usually green rolling fields surrounding the ancient stone circle at Stonehenge have become almost as pale as the path around the prehistoric site.As BBC Verify previously reported parts of the country are suffering from "vegetation stress" where the development and growth of plants, grass and crops can be severely affected.Vegetation turning brown, even on this scale, does not mean the plants have disappeared or died, as grass, shrubs and some trees can recover once rainfall returns, provided their root systems remain intact.Experts have said the combination of next-to-no rainfall and prolonged hot weather is likely to cause significant issues for the farming industry and could have an impact on agriculture and food prices in the coming months.And perhaps counter-intuitively, prolonged dry weather can raise the risk of flash flooding when it eventually does rain. That is because parched, rock-hard ground may struggle to absorb water at first, so some rainwater may simply run off the surface instead.Scientists also warn the UK is facing a growing risk of water shortages in the decades ahead, driven by human-caused climate change and increased demand.Graphics by Tom Shiel

schema.headline: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show impact of hot, dry summer

title: Russian court bars only anti-war party from standing in parliamentary elections
description: Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled.Yabloko was the
body: Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled.Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine. The case against it was brought forward by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party.Hundreds of people - mostly very young - on Monday had stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place in support of Yabloko, singing songs and waving flags. Videos posted on social media showed that when news of the verdict spread among the crowd, many started chanting: "Shame! Shame!"The lawsuit by the Rodina party accused Yabloko of publicly supporting an extremist organisation by publishing material on its website in support of the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designated as extremist in 2023. Rodina also said Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement after a senior party member had quoted the lyrics of a Soviet-era song - "Let there always be sunshine"  - in an interview. At the hearing, Russia's financial monitoring service also claimed that Yabloko received money through third parties from foreign countries, including Germany and the US.The Kremlin-controlled Central Electoral Commission had approved Yabloko's candidate list in late July. But by then several party members had already been barred from running, including two deputy chairmen and deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was sentenced in June to seven years' imprisonment for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha, Mariupol and other Ukrainian cities. And last week, Yabloko had suffered a cyberattack soon after launching a donations appeal for its election campaign fund.It campaigned under the slogan "For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!" and advocated for a "ceasefire, diplomacy, and peace" and "for a Russia free from fear and political repression".Hundreds gathered outside the Moscow courthouse, chanting "Russia" and "Yabloko" - the Russian word for "apple" - as the eight-hour hearing dragged on. Many carried apples as a sign of support.Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, any remaining opposition to the Kremlin has been crushed.Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences. Because protests are no longer permitted, the Yabloko hearing offered a rare chance for likeminded Russians opposing the war to gather publicly. "For Yabloko. For freedom" was scribbled in chalk on the pavement outside the courthouse.Yabloko has not won Duma seats since 2003 but has contested every election since. Once led by presidential contender Grigory Yavlinsky, it later fractured with allies - expelling the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny in 2007 and criticising him even after he was eventually imprisoned ahead of his death in 2024. Still, Yabloko remained Russia's most consistent anti-war voice, opposing Russia's war on Chechnya, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the invasion of Ukraine.With ruling party United Russia's ratings down to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts and drone strikes, Yabloko's support had been surging. The Central Electoral Commission could have allowed Yabloko to contest the election and initially appeared to be leaning in that direction, potentially to use the party's marginal result in 2021 - when it won just 1.34% of the vote - to show how that the anti-war stance in Russia does not hold much sway. But the government has now appeared to have changed its calculations, as signs of growing dissent over the war in Ukraine emerge.Without a political force that clearly represents the opposition on the ballot, fewer people may be motivated to go to the polls. A low-turnout election, particularly among those who oppose the ruling party, would likely benefit the Kremlin.All 10 other parties taking part in the election either support the war in Ukraine or do not openly criticise it.And although United Russia's ratings appear to be in a deep dive, the Kremlin still has the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election.Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process.

schema.headline: Russian court bars only anti-war party from standing in parliamentary elections

title: Ebola started in DR Congo earlier and officials are playing  catch-up, WHO warns
description: The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health autho
body: The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts. There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder."We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

schema.headline: Ebola started in DR Congo earlier and officials are playing  catch-up, WHO warns

title: Evangelos Marinakis: Nottingham Forest owner sues Crystal Palace over fan banner
description: Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace for a banner unfurled by their fans depicting the Nottingham Forest owner holding a gun to midfielder Morg
body: Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace for a banner unfurled by their fans depicting the Nottingham Forest owner holding a gun to midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White's head.Marinakis' lawyers lodged the defamation claim in the High Court on Monday, with CPFC Limited listed as one of the two defendants. The banner, seen during a 1-1 Premier League draw between the two sides at Selhurst Park last August, read: "Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match-fixing, drug trafficking or corruption."Marinakis has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to such allegations.In November 2025, the Football Association had charged Palace with failing to ensure that supporters did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or provocative way.While the banner was not specified as the reason for the charge, there are strict rules regarding messaging containing defamatory, political and offensive slogans.England international Gibbs-White had come close to leaving Forest last summer after Tottenham appeared to trigger a £60m release clause.But he signed a new contract to stay at Forest and spoke about his decision during an interview alongside Marinakis.Marinakis-owned Forest had taken Palace's place in the Europa League last season after the south London club were relegated to the Conference League for breaking Uefa's multi-club ownership rules.BBC Sport has approached Crystal Palace and Nottingham Forest for comment.

schema.headline: Evangelos Marinakis: Nottingham Forest owner sues Crystal Palace over fan banner

title: Treasury contributed to woman's death, Surrey court hears
description: The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an in
body: The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an inquest has heard.Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.Surrey Coroner's Court heard the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy which would have made clear that if the allegations were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.A spokesperson for the Treasury said it was "considering the findings carefully".In a statement to the press, Moffat's family said they believed the Treasury failed in its duty of care."When she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced her career and reputation had been destroyed," they added.The inquest, in which a conclusion of suicide was recorded, heard that on 19 May Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.She was told of allegations she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job.Moffat, from London, denied this.She was informed that no final decision had been taken as to how the allegations would be handled but that it may be by way of a formal investigation or disciplinary meeting.On asking if she would lose her job, assistant coroner Anna Crawford said the senior manager told Moffat she "could not predict the outcome at this stage".Shocked and upset, Moffat cried, and it was agreed she did not have to work for the rest of the day.She texted a friend, the court heard, to say she thought she would be sacked.Moffat then spoke to her mother on the phone, who tried to reassure her, and it was decided she would stay at her parents' house.The next day she took her own life.Crawford said if written policy had been followed, instead of attending the 19 May meeting, Moffat would have been sent a letter which would have advised the likely penalty, if the allegations were proven, was a written warning.During the inquest, evidence was heard that the fact-finding meeting was standard practice at the Treasury and other departments, which Crawford said was a "matter of concern".She said she would be sending a Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report to the Treasury, the head of the civil service and Acas.Moffat's family said: "Our hope has always been that some good can come from this tragedy. "We therefore welcome any recommendations made by the coroner aimed at preventing other families from experiencing the heartbreak we have endured."The family said it hoped a PFD report would lead to "meaningful changes" in how disciplinary processes are conducted and how employees' welfare is safeguarded."Nothing will bring Chloe back. She was a much-loved daughter, sister and friend, and the loss we feel every day is immeasurable," they added.The Treasury said: "We continue to mourn Chloe's passing as a colleague and friend. Our thoughts remain with her family and friends."We take the coroner's concerns extremely seriously and recognise it is important to act quickly. We are now considering the findings carefully."We have introduced improvements to guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements but recognise we must continue to take action to prevent this happening again."If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.Follow BBC Surrey on Facebook, external, on X, external, and on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

schema.headline: Treasury contributed to woman's death, Surrey court hears

title: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia
description: At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said. They confirmed one ch
body: At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said. They confirmed one child was among those killed, with 75 more people injured as drones hit Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces said the city's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit.It is one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. Kyiv has recently stepped up its long-range strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine.The strike on Nizhnekamsk lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, according to local sources. Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. According to Russian news agency RIA, most of the victims had been staying in a hostel at the time of the attack, and Russia's Investigative Committee said that "civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present" where the drones struck. The BBC has not independently verified this information. Moscow said that "all those involved in the attacks" would "face inevitable and severe punishment".Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit once - on 12 June. "The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation. The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased, while Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belayev said the deaths had been a "a tremendous pain for all of us".Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country"."Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive," he added.More than 450 Ukrainian drones were shot down by the Russian air defences overnight across Russia, Moscow said. Elsewhere in Russia, fires broke out when an industrial facility in Siberia's Tyumen region was hit by several falling drones, according to local authorities.Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting.Moscow, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people.

schema.headline: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia

title: Jeff Bezos & Liverpool: Consortium including American advances talks
description: A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.The
body: A consortium including billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has advanced its talks to buy about a 30% stake in Liverpool, BBC Sport has been told.The group is led by British-Indian millionaire businessman Amit Bhatia and also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.Owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed last month that the group had "expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club".Bhatia is the son-in-law of Indian billionaire businessman Lakshmi Mittal and had been a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before relinquishing his stake in the club last month.American businessman Bezos, founder of e-commerce giant Amazon, is the fourth-richest person in the world.According to Forbes, the 62-year-old has an estimated net worth of $256bn (£192bn).FSG, who bought Liverpool in a £300m deal in 2010, previously sold a minority stake in the Anfield side to global sports investment firm Dynasty Equity. BBC Sport contacted FSG about the latest developments, but they had no further comment.In January, Liverpool became the top-earning Premier League club for the first time, according to analysis from financial firm Deloitte. The following month the club announced record revenues of £703m for 2024-25 financial year.

schema.headline: Jeff Bezos & Liverpool: Consortium including American advances talks

title: More than two-thirds of England now in drought
description: Chair of the National Drought Group, Tony Grayling, said that drought conditions will continue to worsen until "significant and sustained rainfall".Th
body: Chair of the National Drought Group, Tony Grayling, said that drought conditions will continue to worsen until "significant and sustained rainfall".The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, as the fifth heatwave of the year intensifies, although there are signs of some rain coming into the UK on Sunday."We know the hot and dry weather is taking a real toll on farming and there will be long-lasting impacts on our environment," Grayling said in a statement, adding that "we need everyone's help in using a little less water to make sure our current water reserves last".The National Drought Group said most of England is now experiencing a flash drought, which "develops very quickly" and is "brought about by a combination of very low rainfall and higher temperatures."Yorkshire and north-east England have been moved to "prolonged dry weather" status, which is the stage before drought. Nowhere in England is now under a "normal" status. Hot weather is continuing, with the UK Health Security Agency issuing amber heat health alerts for all of England apart from the North East from Tuesday at 09:00 BST until Friday at 21:00 BST. An amber alert means significant impacts "are likely" across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.The continued hot and dry conditions increase the risk of wildfires. Dozens of firefighters are currently battling a fire in the New Forest, which earlier on Monday was estimated to be the size of 140 football pitches (247 acres). Follow live updatesScotland and Northern Ireland have not been experiencing drought conditions and are expected to see spells of heavy rain over the week ahead.Scotland does not declare drought, but monitors "water scarcity".While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.Last month, England and Wales saw the driest July since records began in 1836 - while for southern England, it was the driest month ever recorded.South-east England received 1% of the expected average rainfall for July, while some parts of Hampshire, Isle of Wight and West Sussex have not had a rain day for 59 days.All of England is experiencing pressure on water resources, the National Drought Group said.Farmers have reported reduced output after their earliest harvests in 20 years, with the National Farmers Union (NFU) warning that continued dry weather could lead to some food shortages.NFU president Tom Bradshaw said yields of wheat and oats were "very, very poor" this year and warned livestock farmers have had to use their winter feed rations because they have been unable to grow grass.Water Minister Emma Hardy said the government is working to make it easier for farmers to build more on-site irrigation reservoirs, which capture and hold water.Vegetables to get smaller and more expensive due to hot weather, farmers warnOnly 14% of England's rivers are considered to be at normal levels, while 22% are "exceptionally low" - including the River Avon in south-west England and the River Ely Ouse in eastern England.The Environment Agency has warned that low water levels have resulted in potential navigation issues for boats on the Thames, Lark and Ouse.Reservoir levels have also continued to decline, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as "exceptionally low", according to the agency.Warmer water is putting fish under "severe stress," Head of Fisheries at the Angling Trust Mark Owen said, as it holds less dissolved oxygen.Emma Pinchbeck, chief executive of the Climate Change Committee, said the UK is "not prepared at all" for the prolonged dry weather."We're seeing right now with the impacts on farming from this drought and the extreme heat we're experiencing, our infrastructure, our agricultural sector and lots of areas of the economy are not really ready for the weather we now have and how that weather will change up to 2050," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.What has been striking about this summer is not any single record, but the way weather extremes are piling up.Climate change does not cause every heatwave or drought, but it does shift the odds.By raising average temperatures, it makes extreme heat more likely and, when rain fails, increases evaporation and dries soils faster. That creates a feedback - dry ground cools the air less, allowing temperatures to climb still higher.The UK is now seeing the kind of hotter, drier summers climate scientists have long projected, part of a global pattern of heat.  There have been three droughts in the past five years – in 2022, 2025 and now 2026.This year, there have been 34 days with temperatures that have reached 30C or above somewhere in England, including 13 consecutive days in July. Heat extremes are becoming more likely and more intense due to human-caused climate change, the Met Office says.Meanwhile, El Niño - the recurring climate pattern in which unusually warm Pacific Ocean waters can affect weather around the world - is giving global temperatures an additional, natural boost.  The World Meteorological Organisation, the UN agency for climate and weather, says a strong El Niño event is developing and is expected to "dominate global climate patterns" in the coming months.

schema.headline: More than two-thirds of England now in drought

title: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word
description: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikel
body: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.The White House has not officially commented. However, it is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election."We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap.And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza. Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response. An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."In the same statement, the prime minister described President Trump as "the greatest of our friends in the White House" but said that Israel knew "how to stand firm" against unacceptable ideas.In Israel, there is widespread scepticism that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments. The Islamist movement has long seen "armed struggle" as a core precept, its legitimate response to Israeli occupation of Palestinian lands. In recent months, there had been signs of it reasserting its authority in Gaza."Israel can certainly never agree to retreating anywhere where the terrorist group that caused the worst massacres since the Holocaust is still there and is still ruling the Strip," Fleur Hassan-Nahoum, an Israeli commentator and former deputy mayor of Jerusalem told the BBC.She stressed that the "trauma of the Israeli people" from the deadly Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which ignited the devastating Gaza war, should not be underestimated.Any potential concessions for Netanyahu would come at a politically sensitive moment. He is facing an uphill contest in the upcoming general election, scheduled for 27 October. It will be Israel's first since the 7 October assault and three years on, Netanyahu has failed to secure what he vowed: "absolute victory" over Hamas.The former American diplomat and veteran Middle East negotiator, Aaron David Miller, said the Israeli leader is facing "the most consequential election" of his political life. "He's navigating a very fine line between keeping his constituents happy and not angering or alienating President Trump," he told the BBC.For now, he believes the White House recognises the situation and is giving Netanyahu "a pass."  Miller added: "It's hard to believe that you're going to see any serious movement before you have another Israeli government."In the meantime, the Board of Peace has been trying to reassure the Israeli public about the roadmap.The High Commissioner for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov – who led months of delicate negotiations with Hamas – gave an interview to Israel's Channel 12 just hours after Netanyahu's formal rejection of the roadmap."Its goal is to make sure that Gaza is never again a threat to Israeli security and that what happened before, [on] October 7, never happens again," he said.He said the deal takes "a step-by-step approach" meaning: "If there is verified decommissioning of weapons, that they are taken away from the factions and stored and ultimately rendered unusable, Israel then withdraws from Gaza."Ultimately, Mladenov said that nothing was being built "on the basis of trust" but on "verification."Hamas has since indicated that it still remains committed to the roadmap. It called on mediators and the Board of Peace to push for Israel to stick to the terms agreed.The Israeli prime minister has confirmed that talks with the Americans are continuing.Meanwhile heavy pressure from Washington is likely to increase.Trump is also looking at an important election this year – November's midterm elections for the US Congress. His Republican party faces the prospect of heavy losses, with petrol and grocery prices pushed up, in part due to Washington's unpopular five-month-long war in Iran.The US president's own approval rating has tumbled, and he may well demand positive developments in his peace plan for Gaza in an effort to score a much-needed foreign policy win.

schema.headline: Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
description: President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR)
body: President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots."Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said on Monday. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."The Trump administration has long pushed a discredited link between MMR vaccines and autism, but multiple studies have found no link between the two.The federal government does not have the authority to implement the new recommendations. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state level.Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump said that his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox."We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."

schema.headline: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots

title: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades
description: Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russ
body: Finland uses the same track widths as Russia, which are wider than the European standard - a holdover from when the Nordic nation was part of the Russian Grand Duchy in the 19th and early 20th centuries.It is currently in the process of updating its track widths to match the European standard.The new, twice-daily journey to Sweden's Haparanda takes 100-minutes as it hugs the west coast of Finland before crossing the border between the two Nordic neighbours.Passengers travelling on from Haparanda will need to transfer onto a different train to continue southward.But the service makes it possible to travel around 5,000km by rail from Portugal's Algarve to Finland's northernmost train station of Kolari - believed to be the longest train route in Europe.It will also enable a 24-hour train journey between capitals Helsinki and Stockholm.Finland's transport minister said the return of the cross-border service shows cooperation between the two countries was growing "all the time".Elisa Markula, chief executive of Finland's state-owned railway operator VR, said she hopes the service will benefit from a "renaissance" in rail travel across Europe."Train travelling in all Europe is having a renaissance. Also in Finland, our passenger numbers are increasing a lot," Markula told AFP.

schema.headline: New train service connects Finland and Sweden for first time in decades

title: We should smile at our dogs - a new scientific study reveals why
description: Image source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Kun-kun, a very good dog, sits patiently in the brain scanner ByVictoria GillScience correspondentAny dog love
body: Image source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Kun-kun, a very good dog, sits patiently in the brain scanner ByVictoria GillScience correspondentAny dog lover will tell you their canine friend picks up on their mood and emotions.Now scientists have worked out exactly what is going on inside a dog's brain when it sees a human - even a complete stranger - smiling or scowling.Their research involved 14 dogs in total who all sat very still in a brain scanner while they were shown pictures of people's faces.Photographs of happy, smiling human faces made an area of the brain that is associated with reward "light up" with activity.This reward circuitry is the part of the brain that is activated when we enjoy and remember good things, like tasty food or praise.In terms of our own  brains, we often refer to it as the "hit" or "high" that is triggered  by winning a game or even receiving a positive comment on a social media post.Image source, Eniko KubinyiImage caption, The dogs were shown images of strangers' faces with different expressionsIn previous research on dogs, the same brain region has been found to light up when the dogs anticipated a tasty snack, or smelled a familiar person."It controls us having motivation to do things - wanting to do things," explained Laura Cuaya, one of the study's lead researchers at the University of Vienna. "So this finding suggests that happy faces, even those of strangers have a positive value for dogs."Cuaya and her co-researcher, Raúl Hernández-Pérez, went on to investigate how dogs responded to other human emotions - showing dogs images of people displaying happiness, anger, fear, and sadness. But the reward circuitry only responded to happy faces."Dogs can distinguish between positive emotions and all the others, but they don't seem to be able to distinguish between the different negative emotions," Hernández-Pérez, also at the University of Vienna, told BBC News.Image source, Laura Cuaya/University of ViennaImage caption, Researchers Raúl Hernández-Pérez and Laura Cuaya with their dogs Odín and Kun-kun Laura Cuaya and Raúl Hernández-Pérez are partners in research and in life - and something of a canine-cognition power couple. After meeting at secondary school in Mexico the two went on to work together on research projects that have revealed how dogs interpret and respond to human language and behaviour.It is work that has revealed insights into the biology underlying the unique relationship between humans and their dogs.The couple's own border collies, Odín and Kun-kun, have taken part in several of their research projects - including this one. And the couple recruited other dogs - and their owners - for their studies by politely approaching people in the dog park."If we saw someone with a dog that was the right size [for the scanner] - and looked calm and like it was well trained, we'd ask if they would be interested in helping," recalled Hernández-Pérez.How humans changed dogs' brainsImage source, Laura CuayaImage caption, Odín and Kun-kun examine their own brain scans Cuaya explained that, from a neuroscience perspective, "the dog's brain is quite fascinating"."They are really good at understanding emotions in humans - a species that is completely different from them."This research is building a picture of exactly how thousands of years of living alongside humans has made this possible by moulding and changing dogs' brain circuitry."When we compare humans with other primates, we are looking at abilities that may have come from a common ancestor," Cuaya added."With dogs, the story is totally different. They followed a very different evolutionary path, but through domestication, they developed the social abilities needed to understand and cooperate with us."Cuaya and Hernández-Pérez also hope their findings will help show people to communicate more effectively with their own beloved canine companions."We can reward our dogs with treats, but also reward them with happiness," said Cuaya. "So we should smile at the dogs - even at random dogs in the street."The findings are published in the journal iScience, external.

schema.headline: We should smile at our dogs - a new scientific study reveals why

title: How alleged cartel leader Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland
description: Armed police took up positions at the entrances to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin, as the plane carrying Daniel Kinahan approached the city.On t
body: Armed police took up positions at the entrances to the Special Criminal Court in Dublin, as the plane carrying Daniel Kinahan approached the city.On the steps of the building, journalists from Irish and international media tracked the flight online.The Irish government had sent its jet to Dubai.It is usually used to transport ministers, but it left the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with a suspected crime boss on board.The doors of the court opened around half an hour after the aircraft landed at a military airfield nine miles (14km) away.As reporters went through security, we heard the sound of sirens outside - indicating the arrival of the accused.The courtroom filled up over the next 45 minutes - as detectives, prosecutors, and some members of the public took up seats along with the media.From the moment Kinahan entered the dock, until he was led out 13 minutes later, almost everyone was looking towards him - and the proceedings were accompanied by constant typing from the press benches.Complex international investigations, and diplomacy, had led to this moment.Kinahan was charged with a single offence - directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 2015 and April 2017.He did not have to enter a plea at this stage of the court process.But his lawyers have previously told the BBC that the allegations he is a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.They also said he had no criminal record or convictions.Law enforcement agencies on both sides of the Atlantic believe he is a leading figure in the Kinahan Organised Crime Group.The gang began as a street drug dealing operation in Dublin in the 1980s. From there, it became an international player in organised crime.It has been linked to drug trafficking, money laundering, and murder.The former deputy director of the UK's National Crime Agency, Roy McComb, said the group had grown globally because it had the "ambition and drive" to do so.McComb told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the Kinahan group had created links with other organisations from South America, Eastern Europe, Pakistan and Afghanistan, who were involved in the "wholesale distribution" of drugs.He said the cartel became "the go-to organised crime group to move large quantities of narcotics around Europe".McComb explained they were "seen to be a threat to the stability of the US dollar", because they were trading in the currency.In 2022, the US offered a reward of $5m (€4.3m; £3.7m) for information about Kinahan, his father Christopher Senior and brother Christopher Junior.The organisation had previously come to more widespread global media attention in 2016, as the result of a vicious feud with another Irish gang known as the Hutch organisation.During that year, Kinahan was targeted by gunmen at a boxing weigh-in at a hotel in north Dublin.Mobile phone footage of the shooting captured the chaos and brutality of the violence.One man was murdered in that incident. During months of gangland violence, 18 people were killed.Kinahan left Ireland shortly after the attempt on his life.The Irish government put a major diplomatic effort into negotiating an extradition treaty with the UAE, which was signed in 2024.Kinahan is the second person to be brought to Ireland under the terms of the agreement.The first was Sean McGovern, who was described by a judge to be a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan group.In June, McGovern was sentenced to 24 years in jail after pleading guilty to two charges of directing a criminal organisation.Kinahan rose to his feet, with his hands clasped in front of him, when a court official read his charge to him on Sunday.I was sitting about three metres from Kinahan.His appearance was slightly different compared with the well-known photographs of him.He wore plain clothes, including a black hoodie, and glasses.He spoke several times during the hearing, when one of the three judges addressed him directly.His tone was polite.He indicated he would decide later whether he would come to court in person for the next hearing on 5 October, or appear via video link from prison.Outside the court, a crowd of more than 100 people were waiting to see a police convoy carry him away at speed.The prosecution has formally commenced.

schema.headline: How alleged cartel leader Daniel Kinahan returned to Ireland
